title: SA in Numbers
text:
How we work

Numbers first. Short text, clear charts, no opinions on policy.
Uncertainty shown. Estimates come with ranges, and every story says what the data can’t tell us.
Open. Every chart links to its data and the code that made it.

title: South Africa’s temperature, day by day
South Africa’s temperature, day by day
section: What the data can’t tell us
text:
What the data can’t tell us


These are modelled temperatures, not weather-station readings. NASA POWER (MERRA-2) combines satellite data, weather observations and a weather model on a grid of roughly 50 km. It suits comparing years with each other; local station values will differ.
The latest weeks are provisional. NASA fills recent weeks with a near-real-time model and replaces them with its long-term record every few months, so recent values can shift a little.
One national number hides big differences. The Lowveld, the Karoo and the coast can have very different days; this is the average over the whole country.
A year so far is not a full year. Ranks for the current year compare the same dates in every year, and can change as the year goes on.

title: South Africa’s temperature, day by day
text:
Method

Temperature: daily mean air temperature at 2 m (T2M) from NASA POWER at 114 points one degree apart covering South Africa (Lesotho and Eswatini excluded), averaged with weights for grid-cell area (cosine of latitude).
Lines: a 7-day average (each day and the six before it), so the lines show weather spells rather than single days.
Average: the 1991–2020 mean for each day of the year (WMO standard period).
Ranks and anomalies: for the current year, 1 January to the latest date, compared with the same dates in every other year. Full-year values use complete calendar years.
Trend: a straight line fitted to the yearly averages of complete years (ordinary least squares), with its 95% confidence interval. Year-to-year swings are large, so the trend explains only part of the variation (r² = 0.19).
This year’s estimate: the 1991–2020 yearly average plus this year’s difference from normal so far. An average of January to November alone would leave out December and look too cool.
Warming since the 1980s: average of the last ten full years minus the average of 1981–1990 (+0.6°C).

title: El Niño summer tracker 2026/27
section: What the data can’t tell us
text:
What the data can’t tell us


El Niño raises the odds of a dry, hot summer; it does not guarantee one. The very strong 1997/98 event brought near-normal rain to much of the summer rainfall region, while 2015/16 brought widespread drought. Both are shown above for that reason.
Rainfall is estimated from satellites and rain gauges, not read from every gauge. CHIRPS blends satellite estimates with station records on a 5 km grid. It is good at comparing this season with its own past, and weaker for exact local totals, especially for single thunderstorms.
The latest weeks are preliminary. Preliminary CHIRPS uses fewer gauges; final values replace them about three weeks after each month ends, so recent figures can change.
Heat figures are modelled. NASA POWER (about 50 km) fills recent weeks with a near-real-time model and replaces them every few months.
Each region is an index of 5 to 12 sites, not every farm. Rain falls patchily in summer, and one storm can make a district wetter than its region.
Recent El Niño index values are provisional and can be revised for up to two months.
Dam totals cover only the dams in the DWS weekly report, weighted by their capacity.

Season: 1 October to 30 April for the summer-rainfall regions; 1 April to 30 September for the Western Cape. Normal: the 30 seasons starting 1991 to 2020.
Rain: CHIRPS v3 5-day totals (final where available, otherwise preliminary), the mean of a 0.25° window around each of the region’s sites, summed from the start of the season. Western Cape winter rain uses CHIRPS monthly totals. Until 21 November 2026 the tracker used NASA POWER rain; a check against CHIRPS showed its near-real-time rain missed early-November storms, so we switched.
Heat: daily maximum temperature (T2M_MAX) from NASA POWER.
Summer rain index: each summer region’s rain so far as a share of its normal full-season total, averaged with each region counted equally, so the wet east does not swamp the dry west.
Hot day: daily maximum above the site’s own 90th percentile for that time of year (1991–2020, ±7-day window). By construction, a normal season has about one hot day in ten. Counted over 1 October to 30 April in every region, including the Western Cape.
Ranks compare the same dates in every season since 1981/82, the start of the NASA POWER record.
Do the regions hold together? For each pair of sites we correlate their seasonal rain totals since 1981 (Spearman’s r). Sites should move more with their own region than with any other, and a blind cluster analysis should find the same groups. The check is rerun with every change to the site list (tests/check_regions.R).
El Niño strength: NOAA’s Relative Oceanic Niño Index (RONI). An event is five or more overlapping three-month seasons at +0.5 °C or above.
Dams: DWS Weekly State of Reservoirs, % full weighted by full supply capacity.

title: About and methods
text: SA in Numbers publishes South African statistics as charts, short videos and open datasets. The aim is to show what the numbers say, how sure we can be, and what they can’t tell us.

title: About and methods
text:
Principles

Official and reputable sources first. Each chart names its source and the date the data was downloaded.
Modelled estimates are labelled. Where we estimate, project or fill gaps, the chart says so and shows a range. Our estimates are never presented as official statistics.
No cherry-picking. Comparison periods are chosen before a tracker starts and kept for its whole run.
Corrections are public. Errors are fixed in place, with a dated note in the story’s update log.

title: About and methods
text:
Methods
Each story uses whatever method fits its data: simple summaries, regression, time-series models, or Bayesian models where data are sparse. Every story page describes its method and links to the code.
